sections.source_note: Lec 4 pp. 16–45 (model Lec 4 pp. 19–23; scalar gain Lec 4 pp. 25–31; fusion Lec 4 pp. 33–44; assumptions Lec 4 p. 45).
sections.content:
What the filter is for (Lec 4 pp. 17–18). Kalman's method estimates a state recursively from noisy measurements. Used for sensor fusion, it combines dynamic, low-level, redundant data in real time. If the system is linear and the process and sensor noises are white Gaussian, the estimates are unique and statistically optimal. Because it is recursive, it needs no large data store. Applications include object recognition from image sequences, robot navigation, multi-target tracking and inertial navigation.

The model (Lec 4 pp. 19–21).
$$x(t+1)=\Phi(t)x(t)+B(t)u(t)+G(t)w(t),\qquad z(t)=H(t)x(t)+v(t).$$
Here $x$ is the state ($m\times1$), $\Phi$ the state-transition matrix, $u$ a known input, $w$ process noise, $z$ the $n$ measurements, $H$ the measurement matrix and $v$ measurement noise. $w$ and $v$ are uncorrelated, zero-mean white Gaussian sequences with covariances $Q$ and $R$.

The filter equations (Lec 4 pp. 22–23). The update corrects the prediction with the innovation $z-H\hat x$:
$$\hat x(t|t)=\hat x(t|t-1)+K(t)\,[z(t)-H(t)\hat x(t|t-1)],\qquad K(t)=P(t|t-1)H^{\mathsf T}\,[HP(t|t-1)H^{\mathsf T}+R]^{-1},$$
$$P(t|t)=P(t|t-1)-K(t)H(t)P(t|t-1).$$
The prediction pushes the estimate and its error covariance forward:
$$\hat x(t+1|t)=\Phi\hat x(t|t)+Bu(t),\qquad P(t+1|t)=\Phi P(t|t)\Phi^{\mathsf T}+GQG^{\mathsf T}.$$
Start from $\hat x(0|0)=\hat x_0$ and $P(0|0)=P_0$. Here $P(t|t-1)$ is the covariance of the prediction error.

Deriving the gain, scalar case (Lec 4 pp. 25–31). Model: $x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k+w_k$, $z_k=Hx_k+v_k$, with noise variances $Q$ and $R$. The slides use the one-step predictor form $\hat x_{k+1}=A\hat x_k+Bu_k+K_k[z_k-H\hat x_k]$. The design principle is to choose $K_k$ to minimise the variance of the new estimation error.

1. Error: with $\tilde x=x-\hat x$, subtracting gives $\tilde x_{k+1}=(A-K_kH)\tilde x_k+w_k-K_kv_k$.
2. Variance: $\tilde x_k$, $w_k$ and $v_k$ are uncorrelated, so cross terms vanish and $P_{k+1}=(A-K_kH)^2P_k+Q+K_k^2R$.
3. Minimise: $\partial P_{k+1}/\partial K_k=-2H(A-K_kH)P_k+2K_kR=0$, so
$$K_k=\frac{AHP_k}{H^2P_k+R},\qquad P_{k+1}=\frac{A^2P_kR}{H^2P_k+R}+Q.$$
Completing the square (Lec 4 pp. 29–31) gives the same answer and shows it is a minimum: $P_{k+1}=(H^2P_k+R)\big[K_k-\tfrac{AHP_k}{H^2P_k+R}\big]^2+\dots$.

Reading the gain. As $R\to\infty$ (useless sensor), $K\to0$ and the measurement is ignored. As $R\to0$ with $A=H=1$, $K\to1$ and the estimate jumps to the measurement. A large $P$ (uncertain estimate) also pushes $K$ up.

Predictor form versus filter form. The scalar gain contains $A$ because the slides' recursion predicts one step ahead, while the matrix gain on Lec 4 p. 23 updates first. For the fusion example below the state is constant and noise-free ($A=1$, $Q=0$), so the two forms coincide.

Fusion example: a constant state seen by two sensors (Lec 4 pp. 33–35). The state is an object's shape $x$, constant, so $x(t+1)=x(t)$. Two sensors give $z_1=x+v_1$ and $z_2=x+v_2$, where $v_1,v_2$ are independent, zero-mean Gaussian with variances $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$. They can be processed together (batch) or one after the other (sequential).

Batch (Lec 4 pp. 36–40). Use one gain per residual: $\hat x_{k+1}=\hat x_k+K_1(z_1-\hat x_k)+K_2(z_2-\hat x_k)$. The error is $\tilde x_{k+1}=(1-K_1-K_2)\tilde x_k-K_1v_1-K_2v_2$, so
$$P_{k+1}=(1-K_1-K_2)^2P_k+K_1^2\sigma_1^2+K_2^2\sigma_2^2.$$
Setting both partial derivatives to zero gives $(1-K_1-K_2)P_k=K_1\sigma_1^2=K_2\sigma_2^2$ and
$$K_1=\frac{P_k\sigma_2^2}{\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2+P_k(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)},\qquad K_2=\frac{P_k\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2+P_k(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)}.$$
Each sensor's gain is proportional to the other sensor's variance, so the noisier sensor gets less weight. Lec 4 p. 36 also asks what happens with a single gain shared by both residuals; see the practice item.

Sequential (Lec 4 pp. 41–42). Take sensor 1's reading as the prior, $\hat x_0=z_1$ with $P_0=\sigma_1^2$. When $z_2$ arrives, apply one scalar update with $A=H=1$, $Q=0$ and measurement noise $\sigma_2^2$:
$$\hat x=z_1+\frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}(z_2-z_1)=\frac{\sigma_2^2}{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}z_1+\frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}z_2.$$
The slide labels this $R=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\sigma_2^2)$, but in the scalar step only $\sigma_2^2$ plays the role of $R$. The result is the same. With no prior information the batch gains tend to these same weights.

Why fusion helps (Lec 4 pp. 43–44). The fused variance is
$$V(\hat x)=\Big(\frac{\sigma_2^2}{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}\Big)^2\sigma_1^2+\Big(\frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}\Big)^2\sigma_2^2=\frac{\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2}{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2},$$
which is smaller than either $\sigma_1^2$ or $\sigma_2^2$. Equivalently $1/P=1/\sigma_1^2+1/\sigma_2^2$: information adds. The estimate can be updated again as more readings arrive.

Limits (Lec 4 p. 45). The Kalman filter is optimal only if the system is linear and the noises are unimodal Gaussian. Alternatives for other cases: extended and unscented Kalman filters, particle filters, MCMC, RANSAC. Fusion also gains nothing against a shared bias, because systematic error is not averaged away.
sections.summary: Model $x^+=\Phi x+Bu+Gw$, $z=Hx+v$; $w,v$ white Gaussian, covariances $Q,R$. Update $\hat x(t|t)=\hat x(t|t-1)+K[z-H\hat x(t|t-1)]$, $K=PH^{\mathsf T}(HPH^{\mathsf T}+R)^{-1}$, $P(t|t)=(I-KH)P(t|t-1)$; predict $\hat x^+=\Phi\hat x+Bu$, $P^+=\Phi P\Phi^{\mathsf T}+GQG^{\mathsf T}$. Scalar predictor: $P^+=(A-KH)^2P+Q+K^2R$ → $K=AHP/(H^2P+R)$, $P^+=A^2PR/(H^2P+R)+Q$. $R\to\infty\Rightarrow K\to0$. Two sensors, constant $x$: batch $P^+=(1-K_1-K_2)^2P+K_1^2\sigma_1^2+K_2^2\sigma_2^2$, $K_1\propto P\sigma_2^2$, $K_2\propto P\sigma_1^2$. Sequential: $\hat x=\frac{\sigma_2^2z_1+\sigma_1^2z_2}{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}$, $P=\frac{\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2}{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}<\min\sigma_i^2$, $1/P=\sum1/\sigma_i^2$. Optimal only if linear + Gaussian; bias is not removed.

examples.source_locator: Authored for this bank; formulas from Lec 4 pp. 41–43. Checked with exact fractions both ways (weighted average and gain form).
examples.text: Sequential fusion. Sensor 1 reads $z_1=20$ with $\sigma_1^2=4$; sensor 2 reads $z_2=26$ with $\sigma_2^2=2$. Prior: $\hat x_0=20$, $P_0=4$. Gain: $K=P_0/(P_0+\sigma_2^2)=4/6=2/3$. Estimate: $\hat x=20+\tfrac23(26-20)=24$. Variance: $P=(1-K)P_0=\tfrac13\cdot4=4/3$. Check with the weighted-average form: $\tfrac{2}{6}\cdot20+\tfrac46\cdot26=\tfrac{40+104}{6}=24$, and $\tfrac{4\cdot2}{4+2}=4/3$, which is below both 4 and 2. The more precise sensor 2 pulled the estimate two-thirds of the way.

examples.source_locator: Authored for this bank; scalar recursion from Lec 4 pp. 29–31. Checked with exact fractions.
examples.text: One scalar Kalman step. Let $A=H=1$, $P_k=1$, $R=1$ and $Q=1/2$. Gain: $K=\frac{1\cdot1\cdot1}{1+1}=\tfrac12$. Next variance: $P_{k+1}=\frac{1\cdot1\cdot1}{1+1}+\tfrac12=1$. The measurement halved the uncertainty and the process noise added half back. This balance is the filter's steady state for these numbers.

exercises.source_locator: Lec 4 p. 36 (the slide poses the one-gain question). The solution is agent-derived and was checked symbolically with sympy, including the comparison with the two-gain optimum.
exercises.text: The one-gain variant. Fuse with one gain for both residuals: $\hat x_{k+1}=\hat x_k+K[(z_1-\hat x_k)+(z_2-\hat x_k)]$. Find the optimal $K$ and compare it with two gains. Solution: the error is $\tilde x_{k+1}=(1-2K)\tilde x_k-Kv_1-Kv_2$, so $P_{k+1}=(1-2K)^2P_k+K^2(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)$. Setting $dP_{k+1}/dK=-4(1-2K)P_k+2K(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)=0$ gives $K=\frac{2P_k}{4P_k+\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}$ and $P_{k+1}=\frac{P_k(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)}{4P_k+\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}$. This exceeds the two-gain optimum by $\frac{P_k^2(\sigma_1^2-\sigma_2^2)^2}{(4P_k+\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)(\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2+P_k(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2))}\ge0$. The two are equal only when $\sigma_1=\sigma_2$: one shared gain cannot favour the better sensor.

exercises.source_locator: Lec 4 p. 42 ("Derive the above from first principles"). The solution is agent-derived from the scalar steps on Lec 4 pp. 26–29.
exercises.text: Derive the sequential result from first principles. Solution: prior $\hat x_0=z_1$, so the prior error $\tilde x_0=x-z_1=-v_1$ has variance $P_0=\sigma_1^2$. Update $\hat x=\hat x_0+K(z_2-\hat x_0)$. The error is $\tilde x=(1-K)\tilde x_0-Kv_2$, and since $v_1,v_2$ are independent, $P=(1-K)^2\sigma_1^2+K^2\sigma_2^2$. Then $dP/dK=-2(1-K)\sigma_1^2+2K\sigma_2^2=0$ gives $K=\sigma_1^2/(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)$. Substituting gives eq. (12) and $P=\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2/(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)$.

exercises.source_locator: Authored for this bank from Lec 4 pp. 17, 45.
exercises.text: Why might fusing two sensors fail to beat the better one? Give two reasons. Answer, any two: the noises are correlated, so cross terms do not vanish and the variance formula is wrong; one sensor has a bias (systematic error), which averaging spreads into the estimate instead of removing; the system is nonlinear or the noise is not unimodal Gaussian, so the Kalman filter is no longer optimal (Lec 4 p. 45); the stated variances are wrong, so the weights are wrong.

sections.visual_lesson_html:
Each sensor is a bell curve. Fusion multiplies the evidence: the result is narrower than either, and it sits closer to the sharper sensor.

Not yet sat mock 1? Its long question derives this module's two-sensor result. Sit it first, then read on.

Derive the weights in four lines

1. Estimate $\hat x=w z_1+(1-w)z_2$; the weights sum to 1 so that the estimate is unbiased.

2. Error $\hat x-x=wv_1+(1-w)v_2$, with uncorrelated noises, so $P(w)=w^2\sigma_1^2+(1-w)^2\sigma_2^2$ (Module 5 rules).

3. $P'(w)=2w\sigma_1^2-2(1-w)\sigma_2^2=0\Rightarrow w=\dfrac{\sigma_2^2}{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}$.

4. Substitute: $P=\dfrac{\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2}{\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2}$, which is eq. (12) and Lec 4 p. 43. Each sensor's weight is proportional to the other sensor's variance.

Scalar Kalman gain: why $K=AHP/(H^2P+R)$

The error after one step is $(A-KH)\tilde x+w-Kv$. Its variance $(A-KH)^2P+Q+K^2R$ is a parabola in $K$. Setting the derivative $-2H(A-KH)P+2KR$ to zero gives the gain (Lec 4 pp. 26–29). A large $R$ shrinks $K$: distrust the sensor. A large $P$ grows $K$: distrust the prediction.

Check 1

Sensor 2's variance grows without bound (σ₂² → ∞). What does the fused estimate do?

Check 2

Which situation breaks the claim that the Kalman filter is optimal?
